```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5, fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A network estimated from all sessions describes an average interaction.
When the sessions follow different patterns, such as some in which the
human specifies and the AI executes in long runs and others in which the two
alternate rapidly, the average network describes none of them well. Grouping
the sessions by a known variable (a condition, a phase of a course) is one
answer; when no such variable exists, the groups have to be found from the
sessions themselves. Two families of methods do this. Distance-based
clustering groups sessions whose sequences are similar under a distance
measure. A mixture of Markov chains groups sessions by the transition
process most likely to have generated them, so each cluster is a network in
its own right.

`build_htna()` takes a fitted clustering of an htna network and returns one
heterogeneous network per cluster, each with the actor partition of the
original network. The result is a grouped network, the same kind of object
that `build_htna(..., group = )` returns, so every function that works on
cohorts works on clusters. This guide fits both kinds of clustering, shows
how to choose the number of clusters, and compares the resulting cluster
networks.

```{r package}
library(htna)
```

## Data

`human_ai` holds 429 sessions of human-AI pair programming; each row is one
coded event.

- **Session**: `session_id`; the unit that is clustered.
- **Code**: `code`; six human and six AI codes.
- **Actor type**: `actor_type`, `"Human"` or `"AI"`.
- **Order**: `order_in_session`.

The clusterings start from the htna network of all sessions, which carries
the sequences and the actor partition.

```{r build}
data(human_ai)
net <- build_htna(human_ai, actor_type = "actor_type")
```

## Clustering sessions by sequence similarity

`Nestimate::build_clusters()` computes a dissimilarity between every pair of
sessions (Hamming distance by default) and partitions them with
partitioning around medoids into `k` clusters.

```{r distance-fit}
fit_distance <- Nestimate::build_clusters(net, k = 2, seed = 1)
fit_distance
```

The two clusters hold 288 and 141 sessions, but the partition is weak: the
average silhouette is 0.300, and the second cluster has a mean
within-cluster distance of 93.6 against 36.3 for the first. The
per-cluster diagnostics make the problem explicit.

```{r distance-diagnostics}
Nestimate::cluster_diagnostics(fit_distance)
```

The second cluster has a negative silhouette (-0.215): on average its
sessions are closer to the other cluster's medoid than to their own. It is a
remainder of long, dissimilar sessions rather than a coherent group, which
is common for Hamming distances on sequences of very different lengths.

## How many clusters?

`Nestimate::cluster_choice()` fits the distance-based clustering for a
range of `k` and reports the silhouette and the cluster sizes.

```{r distance-choice}
Nestimate::cluster_choice(net, k = 2:4)
```

The highest silhouette (0.756 at `k = 2`) belongs to a partition that
separates 11 sessions from the other 418, a ratio of 38 between the largest
and the smallest cluster. A high silhouette for a small satellite and one
large cluster does not describe two kinds of collaboration, so the size
column has to be read with the silhouette. Neither criterion supports a
distance-based clustering of these sessions.

## Clustering sessions by their transition process

`Nestimate::cluster_mmm()` fits a mixture of first-order Markov chains with
the EM algorithm. Every session receives a posterior probability of
belonging to each component, and each component has its own transition
matrix.

```{r mmm-fit}
fit_mmm <- Nestimate::cluster_mmm(net, k = 2, seed = 1)
fit_mmm
```

The two components hold 280 and 149 sessions. The average posterior
probability of the assigned component is 0.921 (0.932 and 0.902 per
cluster), and the classification error is 7.9%, so the sessions are
assigned with confidence. `Nestimate::compare_mmm()` compares mixtures with
different numbers of components.

```{r mmm-choice}
Nestimate::compare_mmm(net, k = 2:3, seed = 1)
```

BIC and ICL both prefer two components (BIC 74,430 against 74,843), while the
log-likelihood and AIC improve slightly with a third. The two-component
mixture is the model to interpret.

## One network per cluster

`build_htna()` turns either fit into a grouped network, one heterogeneous
network per cluster. The fit is not rerun; the assignments are those of the
fit.

```{r mmm-networks}
clusters <- build_htna(fit_mmm)
as.data.frame(summary(clusters), what = "actor_pairs")
```

Both cluster networks have the same actor partition, and all 36 edges of
every actor-pair block are non-zero. The weights of a cluster network are the
fitted transition probabilities of its mixture component, which give every
transition a non-zero probability, including the transitions never observed
in the data. The networks are drawn side by side:

```{r mmm-plot, fig.height = 4.5}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(1, 1, 3, 1))
plot_htna(clusters)
par(op)
```

The distance-based fit is converted in the same way, with
`build_htna(fit_distance)`.

## How do the clusters differ?

`compare_htna()` compares every pair of clusters and summarizes the
differences by actor-pair block.

```{r compare}
comparison <- compare_htna(clusters)
comparison
```

The two transition processes are more different than the early and late
sessions of the [Comparing networks](comparing-networks.html) guide: the
correlation of their edge weights is 0.877 and the mean absolute difference
0.0336. The actor-pair table locates the differences (`Cluster 1` minus
`Cluster 2`). A human code is followed by another human code with a
probability about 0.040 lower in the first cluster (six target codes times
-0.00666 per cell) and by an AI code correspondingly more often, and an AI
code hands back to the human about 0.027 more often (6 x 0.00449). The
first cluster is the more alternating collaboration. The largest single
difference, 0.268, lies in the AI-to-AI block. The similarity, correlation
and distance measures of the two weight matrices are returned with
`what = "metrics"`.

```{r compare-metrics}
as.data.frame(comparison, what = "metrics")
```

A permutation test of the same pair asks whether the differences exceed
what random splits of the sessions produce. Because the clusters were
formed to differ, a significant result is expected and confirms only that
the mixture separated distinct processes; the useful output is where the
differences lie.

```{r compare-permutation}
perm <- permutation_htna(clusters, iter = 200, seed = 1)
perm
plot_htna_diff(perm)
```

Both global statistics reach the smallest p-value attainable with 200
permutations (0.00498), and 66 of the 144 edges differ at an unadjusted
p-value below 0.05; green edges in the plot are stronger in the first
cluster, red edges in the second. The [Comparing
networks](comparing-networks.html) guide explains the three comparisons in
detail.

## Which clustering to use

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| Group sessions by the similarity of their sequences | `Nestimate::build_clusters()`, then `build_htna(fit)` |
| Group sessions by the transition process that generated them | `Nestimate::cluster_mmm()`, then `build_htna(fit)` |
| Choose `k` for distance-based clusters | `Nestimate::cluster_choice()` (read sizes with the silhouette) |
| Choose `k` for a mixture | `Nestimate::compare_mmm()` (BIC, ICL) |
| Check one fitted partition | `Nestimate::cluster_diagnostics()` |
| Compare the cluster networks | `compare_htna()`, `permutation_htna()` |

For heterogeneous networks the mixture of Markov chains is usually the more
informative choice, because its clusters are defined by transition
processes, the same object the networks describe.

```{r restore-options, include = FALSE}
options(old_options)
```
